subtitle: Here's What I've Been Buying and Selling
title: June 2026 Portfolio Review
description: Here's What I've Been Buying and Selling
body_html:
Disclaimer: By reading this article, you acknowledge and agree to the terms and conditions

You’re not losing your mind. If it feels like things are crazy, that’s because they really are. As crypto seemingly fades into irrelevancy, its knee-jerk moves have insidiously become commonplace to metals, megacaps, and even traditionally boring sectors such as consumer staples and insurance.

Part of the reason, to borrow a phrase from the President, is because “everything is computer”. Gross hedge fund exposure and median short interest are near record highs as investors pile into the AI Trade and discard everything else.

The chart above from Goldman Sachs’s Prime Brokerage Desk depict stunning gross and net concentration in Semis, and the continued pile-on into the AI trade has caused cross-sector correlations to go haywire. To see that exemplified, look no further than the insurance sector. For the first time ever, the insurance sector (KIE) is negatively correlated with the S&P on a 40 day rolling basis.

The S&P Low Volatility Index has similarly become negatively correlated with the S&P.

It’s not like AI has magically become the ultimate enemy of insurers, banks, and consumer staples businesses in the span of two months, rather, these wild moves and cross-sector correlations are the result of positioning: people are pressing the pedal to the metal on the AI trade by paring down everything else, and when they degross, the unwind gets violent quickly. From Wednesday June 3rd through Wednesday June 10th, the Semiconductor Index was down 10% while Banks rallied up 5%. If you’re looking for an explanation, look no further than the fact Institutional positioning in Financials started the month at the 0th percentile (in relative terms since 2010), while Information Technology started the month off at the 99th percentile (source: Morgan Stanley Prime Brokerage Desk).

Given the recent volatility, I think it’s fair to say many investors are aggressively exposed with complicated positions. The question is, what should we do?

I think the answer is clear: keep things simple until everyone calms down.

Since April I’ve been trying to do as little as possible and avoid working myself up into a frenzy. If you interpreted every Iran or Tech headline at face value, you’d wind up in the insane asylum.

I think the same goes for deciding whether to buy the dip. A lot of recent market action seems to be driven by recency bias, people looking at where a stock was merely two or three days ago, and using the differential to decide whether to go “all in” or “all cash”.

I think the memory names exemplify this well. In the depths of April, Turboquant nearly made its way onto the terrorist watchlist - it was panic like never before. If you asked stunned memory bulls (including myself) if they’d be willing to take off some Micron at $550 or $600 if it ever returned, the answer would’ve been an clear yes. “Oh if you let me get out of this hole, I’ll never take risks like that again”.

Now, Micron has more than tripled to $900, yet people aren’t merely maintaining their positions, they’re aggressively piling in because it was $1,080 a few days ago. If you’re scooping up shares because you believe Micron will hit a $30 a quarter run rate by Q3 and memory is no longer cyclical, I tip my hat to you, but otherwise, I think it’s okay to say “You know what, it’s up 200% YTD, a little volatility is to be expected and I don’t need to buy this dip”.

This year the volatility has been immense. The crown has rotated from Gold and Silver connoisseurs to Small Cap Oil Experts to Korean Memory Superfans, over and over and over again. Rather than chase, I think the best thing to do is just purchase reasonably priced equities with decent growth prospects and capital return potential, and let time put in some work.

My Portfolio is relatively untouched since the last update in April, but I have been adding to a few existing positions and collaring a few I view most at risk. Here’s what I’ve been up to.

Portfolio Changes

Reduce CBL & Associates (CBL)

The CBL thesis has played out exactly as we expected: the company refinanced its term loan, opportunistically disposed of assets, occupancy stabilized, and cash returns to shareholders have surged. The stock has significantly re-rated from the entry of $28.20, and on a total return basis, has now doubled. It’s clear the market is appreciative of the steps CBL has taken.

With annual FFO of around $7.10 a share, the question becomes what multiple will the market assign to CBL? On one hand, with the term loan out of the way and much of the new refinancing offered as “interest-only”, you can argue the balance sheet is substantially de-risked and an 8-9x multiple is warranted. On the other hand, CBL specializes in lower-tier Class C and Class B Real Estate, and I think it’s unlikely CBL ever trades near peers. At $50 a share (7.1x FFO), I think the company is unlikely to be repurchasing many shares, so the trade has transformed from “deep value” into a momentum position where the only real uncertainty is how the market perceives the company.

After the recent run up CBL ballooned into one of my largest positions, and I wanted to recycle capital into ideas I find most attractive. I’ve trimmed my position significantly, and have kept a small portion of my realized profits invested in the company.

Put Protection on Google (GOOGL)

I purchased July 355 Strike Puts on my entire Google position. Google is my favorite member of the MAG7, and while I don’t like equity raises, I think Google is extremely judicious in their capital allocation (in fact their entire recent equity raise is still less than the 240 Million shares they repurchased in 2025 at an average price of $189).

I think you could also argue that if anyone can gauge attractive opportunities to deploy capital, it’s probably Google given they have a rapidly growing cloud business, their own AI ambitions, significant experience in Data Centers, and even design their own TPUs. The proof is in the numbers, Google Cloud Operating Income has surged from just $191 Million in 2023 Q1, to $6.6 Billion in 2026 Q1.

With such a bullish backdrop, why sprinkle in put protection? I believe the answer is that the prospect of large equity raises is a slap in the face to the average MAG7 bull. For years, the MAG7 has been the exemplar of “capital light”. Tech companies were able to direct hundreds of billions in cash flow towards share repurchases, building an image of “businesses that no one could compete with”. Now, we have Meta apparently pondering raising capital at 17x earnings (a discount to the broader market), and I think investors are shocked. “Why would Meta even consider that?” On a side note, I think Meta’s reasoning is relatively unrelated to the stock price and that Mark Zuckerberg simply doesn’t care about how much he is worth and wants to do whatever it takes to catch up (remember the Metaverse?).

Still, I think the onslaught of capital raises from Google, Oracle, SpaceX, and potentially Meta is spooking investors, and I’d rather be positioned in capex beneficiaries such as Hynix, Samsung, and Kioxia. Google has doubled since the initial entry, and I’ve purchased July 355 Strike Puts for $10 on my position to cap downside in the near-term. I have zero intention of getting rid of my Google, if the puts are in the money close to expiration, I will roll them or cash them in.

Protective Collar on Powell (POWL), Comfort Systems (FIX), and IES Holdings (IESC)

The infrastructure basket has been on an incredible run this year. Comfort Systems is up 97%, IES Holdings 87%, and Powell Industries 162%.

Valuations are a little lofty, and I’m worried about a “stairs up, elevator down” level implosion. On one hand, I think the analyst estimates for FIX (NTM Consensus EPS: $44.16, I am closer to $60) and IESC (NTM Consensus EPS: $20.15, I am closer to $22) are lowballed, and that all three stand to gain significantly from the surge in Data Center construction. On the other hand valuations are high and the chart (at least for Comfort Systems), seems to suggest momentum is slowing.

I think the best way to maintain some skin in the game while eliminating left-tail risk is by collaring these names on a monthly basis, and leaving yourself +/- 10% in either direction. Currently, I have Comfort Systems collared via long June 1780 Puts and short June 2200 Calls, IESC collared via long June 660 Puts and short June 810 Calls, and Powell Industries collared via long June 260 Puts and short June 340 Calls. The market has moved down since I collared these positions after May expiry, but to illustrate how effective these collars can be, you could sell a July IESC 840 Call and purchase a July IESC 650 Put for roughly $1, capping downside at 11% while leaving 15% further upside. I have no intention of letting IES Holdings go, I consider it to be best in class and I really like the leadership alignment (Chairman owns $4 Billion) and their differentiated strategy of buying out suppliers and custom parts makers. Closer to the June expiry next week, I will monetize the collars if any of the strikes are in the money, and roll to July. I’m not turning bearish on these names, but I think the pattern they exhibit is a clear slow trend up with the potential of a shock move down, so collaring at +/- 10% leaves significant upside while reducing left-tail risk.

SPX Hedge

Earlier this week, I put 0.25% of my Portfolio into SPX 7300 Puts. I am by no means a bear, but given the great YTD start and chaos we are seeing, I want to have some downside protection here in the event the Iran situation blows out of proportion over the next 5 weeks. The 0.25% allocation reduces my overall Portfolio Delta to the S&P by about 6% at current levels. I dislike shorting the market overall to reduce exposure in this type of chaotic environment, just as we saw after “Liberation Day”, you could get an “Iran and US Announce Stunning Agreement” headline and the market surges 4% in a matter of minutes, burning a short position you intended to use to simply hedge your Portfolio. As a result, I think it makes sense to express any cautious view via puts.

Position Increase: Vistance Networks (VISN)

Vistance Networks (+34% YTD) has quickly become a high conviction trade for me. I wrote extensively about it here, and I am getting even more interested in it. At current prices, the market is ascribing a stunningly low valuation to the stub, its Aurora Networks division. Aurora Networks sells DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade gear (nodes, amplifiers, virtualized access) to cable operators like Comcast and Vodafone who increasingly want to squeeze out maximum performance from their existing infrastructure instead of laying fresh fiber. Q1 revenue for Aurora Networks jumped 32%, EBITDA jumped 31%, and the company is increasingly announcing multi-year contracts. With the stub trading at 4.5x EBITDA, versus peers at 6x - 20x, I believe it is too cheap to ignore and have been steadily adding to my position at $12.

New Position: SK Square 402340 KS Equity, and Korea Value Basket: Hyundai Green Food 453340 KS Equity, iM Financial Group 139130 KS Equity, and Hy-Lok 013030 KS Equity

Subsequent to IBKR adding Korean equities, I added SK Square. SK Square is the SK Telecom spin-off whose only asset that really matters is its 22% stake in SK Hynix which comprises 98%+ of NAV. Currently, SK Square trades at a 46% discount to Net Asset Value, providing an opportunity to gain exposure to SK Hynix at a look-through P/E of just 3.5x (applying a 46% discount to SK Hynix’s Forward P/E of 6.5x).

SK Square has a stated goal of closing the discount to Net Asset Value to just 30% by 2027, and I believe it is inevitable the company launches a fresh repurchase program to address the discount. Given Hynix is likely to receive regulatory approval for an ADR later this month and list in the United States in early August, I think it’s possible SK Square sells a portion of its stake back to Hynix to provide shares for the ADR, and uses the cash to further narrow the discount to Net Asset Value.

I’ve also been steadily adding to small positions in Hyundai Green Food, iM Financial Group, and Hy-Lok. All three have performed poorly since my entry in May, Hy-Lok is down 25%, Hyundai Green Foods is down 9%, and iM Financial is down 6%.

Despite the rough start, I’m not concerned. Hyundai Green Foods trades at just 5x forward earnings with a cash balance equal to 40% of the market cap, 10% annual revenue growth, a dividend that is set to double over the next 2 years, and a share repurchase program that is actively being executed. iM Financial Group trades at less than half Tangible Book Value, 5.6x forward earnings, a dividend yield of 4%, and is likely to begin the next phase of its Capital Return initiative later this year via highly accretive repurchases. Hy-Lok reported its strongest quarter in years, is trading around 6x forward earnings, has 19,000 Won in net cash per share (60% of the market cap) and a 4% dividend yield. All three basket components are exquisitely cheap, have a consistent history of growth, and their cash rich balance sheets provide ample room to fund the next wave of dividends and repurchases. I think price drives narrative and that increased investor attention to the Kospi is spilling over to many smaller “value traps” who are finally feeling pressure to initiate capital return initiatives. All three have repurchased decent quantities of shares since 2025, and I think the combination of attractive valuation with steadily improving capital allocation will help them gradually re-rate.

New Position: GMR Solutions

GMR Solutions is the largest ambulance operator in the United States. Its IPO flopped horrendously, the deal priced at just $15 after guiding to a $22-$25 range, and the stock promptly fell to just $10.50 last week. Recently, there have been several initiations of coverage, and while the backdrop for the company is slowing, the stock is trading under 8x 2027 earnings. GMRS is heavily owned by Private Equity (KKR controls 77%), and the story is simple: the company is focused on debt-reduction, and cash will be returned to the shareholders once GMRS’s leverage goals are achieved.

I don’t expect a significant and sudden re-rate, but I do think extremely bullish forecasts from Goldman Sachs ($35) are likely to gather attention, and as Institutional ownership builds, the stock drifts towards a more reasonable multiple (8.5x 2027 earnings would imply $14.40 a share). For now, GMRS is a low-conviction trade for me, and I have saved a lot of capacity to add in the $12 - $12.50 range, where I believe the risk-to-reward is most favorable.

Portfolio Review

Memory, Storage, and Tech (~25% Weight):

The Memory, Storage, and Tech basket benefited significantly from the surge in Memory Positions (Hynix, Samsung, Kioxia), as well as Entravision, which tripled since the last update.

I know there is a heightened level of concern surrounding the AI Names. All too often, we see suave “forecasters” confidently explain why the AI buildout is 100% a bubble, and how it’s all going to end badly. What I think they are conflating, however, is valuation with progress. There is no doubt a few “bottlenecks” trading at 100x sales are loftily valued, and many of these names will probably deliver poor returns over the next few years. I think the AI buildout, on the other hand, will not stop moving forward, and in fact, accelerate sharply.

Only a fraction of the World’s population currently uses AI, and this fraction will continually grow. The signs of AI usage are everywhere: banks and accounting firms are increasingly recruiting smaller “class” sizes as existing employees utilize AI to complete entry level tasks, phone service support from large corporations like Mint Mobile all the way down to local HVAC firms is being provided by AI agents, even earnings calls are featuring AI Clones. I think the fact that neoclouds like Nebius who cater to smaller-sized businesses are not only raising prices but are entirely sold out of capacity is demonstrative of the fact AI is still underpriced relative to the benefit it provides, and as long as this is still the case, AI demand will be insatiable.

Recent reports from tech giants such as Oracle, Meta, Google, and Amazon, hint at record 2027 capex budgets as the buildout continues. Analysts are penciling in $250 Billion for Google in 2027 (versus $180 Billion in 2026), $70 Billion for Oracle in 2027 (versus $50 Billion in 2026), $160 Billion for Meta in 2027 (versus $135 Billion in 2026) and $230 Billion for Amazon in 2027, (versus $200 Billion in 2026). The amounts being spent are immense. Does this mean it is a bubble? In my opinion, no, as long as the hyperscalers see returns on their investments.

Every indication from Google, Amazon, and Microsoft’s cloud divisions shows they see an excellent potential return on their capital and that operating income is booming. The rush to seize this opportunity has been incredibly favorable for suppliers like SK Hynix, Samsung, Micron, Western Digital, and Kioxia.

Not only are many of them receiving pre-payments from eager customers, several, such as SK Hynix, have been approached by customers with offers to procure equipment in exchange for increasing supply. As these capex budgets continue to boom, the cash will flow downstream into the eager hands of Samsung, SK Hynix, Western Digital, Kioxia, and Micron (all of which I own).

People will argue that Memory and Storage is inherently cyclical, and they are right. There is zero doubt in my mind that memory and storage prices eventually cool down. The question is: when?

I think what differentiates this cycle from previous ones is that all of the suppliers are extremely eager to avoid oversupply.

Take Western Digital and Seagate, for example, who dominate the Hard Drive market (Toshiba has a smaller 10% share). As prices surge, both companies have essentially agreed to not increase capacity.

At the JPM Tech conference on May 18th, Seagate’s CEO said in response to capacity:

“If we took the teams off and started building new factories or bringing up new machines, it would just take too long. You would end up more capacity, if you will, but then you’d slow the rate of growth on that technology.” - Dave Mosley, STX CEO

Just a few hours later at the same conference, the Western Digital CFO commented:

“Now, when we look at that, we look at that, do we have to add unit capacity to support plus 25% compound annual growth rate for the next three to five years? The answer is no. We know how to support the strong growth in exabytes of our customers not by adding unit capacity, but through technology and product transitions.” - Kris Sennesael, Western Digital CFO

They might not have said it directly, but the implication is they are happy supply is tight, and they want to keep it that way to maximize profits.

It’s a similar story in DRAM and NAND production. Supply is coming online slowly, but the giants have been extremely disciplined in keeping supply tight and anticipate the supply and demand differential will grow in 2027 despite production increases.

“So currently, just based on pre-booked demand alone, the supply demand gap is looking to widen further in 2027 versus this year. With available capacity under such constrained conditions, we plan to maintain our product mix focus on servers in the second quarter, and we’re expecting DRAM bit growth to increase by single digit percentage QonQ.” - Jaejune Kim, EVP Samsung Electronics Q1 Earnings Call

As a result, I think the question is not whether it is a cycle, but rather, how long the good times will last?

Hynix is trading at 6.5x forward earnings, Micron at 10x, Samsung at 6.3x, and Samsung Preferred at just 4.7x, and the Samsung and Hynix valuations seem reasonable to me. If the memory cycle lasts longer than the mid-2027 peak case many still subscribe to, earnings could be even stronger, providing an additional tailwind.

Unlike previous cycles, I think the current one is driven by insatiable demand from AI models as they become more intelligent, not a slight supply and demand imbalance that can be easily rectified. Just a few years ago, ChatGpt seemed like a funny gimmick, and the videos of Will Smith eating spaghetti were unsettling. Less than four years later, we have AI impersonating CEOs on earnings calls, people “vibe coding” incredible projects in just a few messages, and videos that are so realistic they are indiscernible to the average retiree.

As the AI arms race continues and China jumps into the fray with a rumored 295 Billion Sovereign AI Buildout Fund, I think the downstream beneficiaries like Hynix, Samsung, Kioxia, and Western Digital will continue to rake the cash in. On a side note, I also have a feeling YMTC’s and CXMT’s incremental Chinese DRAM and NAND production will be forced to be sold to Chinese Data Centers in lieu of flooding the International Market, after all, China is a command and control economy and I think they’d prefer to prioritize their AI ambitions over flooding the World with cheaper components.

Within Memory and Storage, I find SK Hynix and Samsung Preferred to be the most attractive. SK Hynix also has significant NAND exposure via their own operations and their 20% stake in Kioxia, and I think by 2028, SK Hynix and Samsung will have a significant chunk of their current market cap in cash. Given the discipline they have shown so far, I think it is likely some of this cash will begin to be returned to the shareholders, and I also think Hynix’s impending listing in the US will drive significant passive flows, should it choose to list on Nasdaq (where it will almost certainly be added to the Nasdaq 100).

Taiwan Semiconductor’s US listing (TSM US) trades at an 18% premium to the local listing (2330 TT). The ADRs are not freely convertible, but I think the premium indicates how US listed names, in particular technology names, tend to trade at a premium as a result of investor inflows. Once Hynix lists in America, I expect a similar inflow to occur, which should provide a nice tailwind.

Despite my overall bullishness on AI and Memory, I also want to keep risk contained. Western Digital, Kioxia, Hynix, and Samsung are extremely correlated, and due to sheer price appreciation they have become a large chunk of my Portfolio. I’ve shorted the DRAM ETF against my positions to cap the overall allocation to 20% of my Portfolio. Once things settle down I will consider taking off some of the hedge.

Entravision has also been on an incredible run. I think right now it is a “prove me” story, investors are eager to see if it can replicate incredible Q1 performance. Until I see further results (the company is reporting in early August), I don’t plan on touching my position, although I have been selling some 10 and 12.5 Strike Calls to harvest a little premium.

AI Infrastructure (~10%)

As discussed above, I am keeping IESC, POWL, and FIX collared within +/- 10% for now.

Banking, Insurance, and Financial Services (~37.5% Weight)

The Banking, Insurance, and Financial Services basket has performed extremely well since the last update. Not only have most of the names bizarrely balanced out sharply negative moves in the S&P, many components such as Marex, Waterstone Financial, Chain Bridge Bancorp, and the Japanese Banks, are trading at record highs.

There have been two significant losers: OSB Group (-17% YTD) and Heritage Insurance (-23% YTD). I’ve been adding to OSB Group in the 490p - 510p range, and Heritage Insurance in the $21 - $22 range, and I find both highly compelling at current prices. Perception surrounding Heritage Insurance is sharply negative, people doubt its ability to return to growth later this year, and overall sentiment regarding the FL specialists is despondent. What I like about this type of setup is that as long as the base case continues and Heritage repurchases shares at 5x forward earnings, the bear case will fall apart and the stock should eventually re-rate. I got slammed on the 20% drop earlier this year (I think it was largely unfair to Heritage given it was entirely weather related), but I also think it is important to put things into perspective.

The stock is up more than 1,000% in the last three and a half years, but the comeback story has been rife with significant drops. I think as long as the company continues to execute, it’s worth giving Heritage some time to prove itself. With Tangible Book Value of $16.21, and likely year end Tangible Book Value of $19 - $20, I believe the $21 - $22 range offers a favorable entry point. On a side note, I think it’s important to note the usual 10b5-1 monthly insider selling that occurs on the 1st of the month did not occur, which I believe is indicative of the stock being so undervalued it isn’t even within range of the pre-determined insider trading plans.

I’ve also increased OSB to 3.5% of my Portfolio (more details here). Share repurchases at the current 6.5x earnings multiple are highly accretive, and I think at just 0.83x Tangible Book Value, a fair amount of “distress” is already priced into the name.

I think the OSB’s 7% dividend, paired with daily repurchases amounting to 7-8 bps of the float, differentiates it from other “value traps” trading at a discount who don’t return cash. OSB’s next report will be in early August, so if you are interested in establishing a position, it might make sense to wait closer to the report as I believe a strong result is the only thing that can “reset” sentiment.

From a technical perspective, I think Marex and Chain Bridge Bancorp are finally breaking out.

Despite the 80% run since position entry last October, Marex still trades at a palatable 12x forward earnings. Its peer, StoneX (previous Portfolio Holding cut in March), now trades at 21x earnings, and I think there is still some room for Marex to close the gap. Given elevated commodity and market volatility, Marex is primed (no pun intended, they also have a Prime Brokerage) to beat earnings, and I think the “growth” crowd is finally beginning to pay attention to it.

Chain Bridge Bancorp set a fresh high today. Given its deposit base is almost entirely zero-cost political deposits from Republican Organizations, I think the prospect of no further rate cuts in 2026, along with a Department of Justice Investigation into JP Morgan for “de-banking” (JP Morgan is the other major bank that caters to Republican Organizations) provides an excellent backdrop. I’ve been getting many questions on Chain Bridge after the recent run up, I still hold my entire position and I think further upside exists to $40 - $45 a share.

Within the basket overall, the names I find most compelling are HRTG between $21 and $22, OSB between 490 - 510, KSPI < $80, ASIC < $20, and IGIC between $23 and $25.

Global Equities and Miscellaneous (~17.5% Weight)

Aside from significantly reducing CBL and initating smaller positions in the Korea Value Basket (Hyundai Green Food, iM Financial Group, and Hy-Lok), I have also been adding to Modern Dental Group (3600 HK), which I originally wrote up last year.

Modern Dental Group is a global manufacturer of dental prosthetics and implants. Despite being headquartered in Hong Kong, the company derives the vast majority of its revenue internationally and operates a network of 80 direct-to-dentist laboratories across Europe, the United States, Australia, and China. The company is consistently expanding into new geographies, pays a sizeable 5% dividend, has grown EPS at a 40% CAGR since 2022, and has a highly aligned management team (founding family owns 50%, with an additional 17% held by Hillhouse Investment Management, an Asian Investment Firm specializing in Healthcare investments).

What really caught my eye, however, was the fact the company has begun repurchasing at a 100,000 shares a day pace for the first time since June 2025. Even though the repurchases are small, Modern Dental Group has a history of excellent capital allocation, and I think the fact they are repurchasing around 5.80 HKD is indicative of the fact they want to support the stock and believe the fair value lies significantly higher. At just 9x earnings with a history of consistent growth and a de-risked business that isn’t tied to interest rates or energy prices, I think it’s worth considering a starter position in Modern Dental Group.

Within Global Equities, Correios De Portugal (CTT PL), Cash Converters (CCV AU) and Itafos (IFOS CN), are all performing poorly, but I remain convicted to them and have been adding to all three recently.

Correios De Portugal, the dominant Portuguese logistics firm that also operates a rapidly growing bank at its thousands of outposts, is now trading at a very reasonable 11x forward earnings. Recent reports indicate financial peers may be interested in acquiring CTT’s Bank, and in the meantime, CTT has expedited the pace of share repurchases to around 60,000 shares a day.

I don’t believe you should follow share repurchases blindly, but I do like to pay attention to the daily repurchase reports as I think they can be used to build a technical setup on top of fundamentals. In this case, CTT is already pretty attractive at 11x forward earnings, and you can also see that the < 6 EUR range is where the company is willing to get aggressive. I’ve been adding in the 5.70 - 5.90 EUR range, and am looking forward to earnings next month.

Cash Converters (originally covered here), continues to trade at 8x forward earnings, a 7% dividend yield, and a slight discount to its own Tangible Book Value. In my opinion, Cash Converters is a growth name masquerading as value setup, it has dozens of franchisees across the globe it is steadily acquiring for 3-5x EBITDA with its organic cash generation. Given its smaller market cap and semi-annual reporting, the stock hasn’t moved much since entry, but I believe a 7% dividend yield paired with a discount to Tangible Book represents an attractive entry point, notwithstanding Cash Converters’ growth prospects which should begin to shine through when it reports in August.

Finally, the largest loser for me this year is Itafos, a small phosphate miner and fertilizer producer who has been heavily impacted by the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz. Sulphuric Acid is a major fertilizer input, and the blockage of Hormuz (which supplies half of the global Sulphuric Acid Supply) has resulted in input prices surging. To compound the chaos, Itafos sells its finished product to a distributor at a 90-day moving average of fertilizer prices, which has led to a double whammy of surging inputs and slowly repricing outputs. The stock is trading at 2.43 CAD, a 20% discount to Tangible Book Value of 3.16, and less than 3x 2025 earnings. Importantly, the company has minimal leverage, a highly aligned owner (Castlelake Management owns 66%), and has a history of returning excess cash via special dividends. Many larger fertilizer producers such as Mosaic have already curtailed output, and I think the opening of the Strait of Hormuz will lead to rapid normalization of sulphur and a slower re-pricing of Phosphate Fertilizer, leading to a double tailwind for Itafos. Right now, at 3x 2025 earnings and a 20% discount to book, the market is pricing Itafos as if the Strait will be permanently closed, but I think eventually the situation will resolve (if not, we are in trouble). Until then, I think the company will continue to operate near break-even, and despite my general rule of cutting anything past a 15% loss, I want to give Itafos some time.

Conclusion

The investors who get hurt most in volatile markets are those who panic-sell the lows or those who leverage up after proclaiming a “bottom” just a week into a drawdown. During these turbulent times, I think it’s ok to say “I don’t know”, and to not react to increasingly “normal” +/- 15% moves.

Over the long-term, I think momentum and growth will continue to outperform value, but I also think the events of the last two weeks demonstrate why having a bit of diversification can come in handy. Ultimately, how you construct your Portfolio shouldn’t simply center around chasing the highest returns, but rather, the level of risk and positioning you are comfortable with. When you are overexposed or uncomfortable, you tend to make worse decisions, and I think it’s ok to sprinkle in less volatile “value” names you feel comfortable holding even if they are likely to have slightly lower long-term returns compared to momentum.

I will continue to post regular updates in the chat, and to those of you participating in the SpaceX IPO, wishing you the best.
